title: Melanchthon: church doctrine is taken from God's revealed sayings, not from demonstrations
pass_a_gloss: And wisely Philip Melanchthon in the preface of the Loci Communes: Doctrine, he says, of the Church is not taken from demonstrations, but from sayings which God by sure and illustrious testimonies handed down to the human race, through which by immense goodness he disclosed himself and his will. And, as in philosophy certain things are sought, and are distinguished from uncertain things, and the causes of certainty are universal experience, principles, and demonstrations: so in the doctrine of the church, the cause of certainty is the revelation of GOD, and it must be considered which sentences have been handed down by God. As this sentence is certain to any sound person, Twice four are eight, for it is natural knowledge, as of principles: so let the articles of faith, the divine threats and promises, be certain and unmoved for us; so let it be certain that for the one doing penitence sins are remitted, that for the sake of the Son of God he is heard, and is made heir of eternal life. But the causes of certainty are diverse. The mind by its own judgment sees the sentence about numbers. But the articles of faith are certain on account of revelation, which has been confirmed by sure and illustrious testimonies of God, as by the resuscitation of the dead, and by many other miracles. But because they are things placed outside the judgment of the human mind, the assent is more languid, which happens because the mind is moved by those testimonies and miracles, and is helped by the Holy Spirit unto assenting.
pass_b_english: And Melanchthon speaks wisely in the preface to the Loci Communes. The doctrine of the church, he says, is not taken from demonstrations, but from sayings that God handed down to the human race by sure and illustrious testimonies — sayings through which, in his immense goodness, he disclosed himself and his will.

Just as philosophy seeks what is certain, separates it from what is uncertain, and names as causes of certainty universal experience, principles, and demonstrations, so in the church's teaching the cause of certainty is the revelation of God, and what must be weighed is which sentences God has handed down.

As any sound mind finds this sentence certain — "Twice four are eight" — because it is natural knowledge, like the knowledge of principles, so let the articles of faith, the divine threats and promises, stand for us certain and unmoved. So let the penitent be certain that sins are remitted, that for the Son of God's sake he is heard, and that he is made an heir of eternal life.

But the causes of certainty differ. The mind sees the sentence about numbers by its own judgment. The articles of faith are certain because of revelation, confirmed by God's sure and illustrious testimonies — the raising of the dead and many other miracles. Yet because these are matters set outside the judgment of the human mind, the assent is weaker: it arises because the mind is moved by those testimonies and miracles and is helped by the Holy Spirit to assent.
source_text: Et sapienter Philippus Melanchthon praefat. L. C. Doctrina, inquit, Ecclesiae non ex demonstrationibus sumitur, sed ex dictis, quae Deus certis & illustribus testimoniis tradidit generi humano, per quae immensa bonitate se & suam voluntatem patefecit. Ac, ut in philosophia quaeruntur certa, & discernuntur ab incertis, & causae certitudinis sunt experientia universalis, principia & demonstrationes: ita in doctrina ecclesiae, certitudinis causa est revelatio DEI, & considerandum est, quae sententiae a Deo traditae sunt. Ut certa est cuilibet sano haec sententia, Bis quatuor sunt octo, est enim naturalis notitia, ut principiorum: ita sint certi nobis & immoti articuli fidei, comminationes & promissiones divinae; ita certum sit, agenti poenitentiam remitti peccata, propter Filium Dei exaudiri se, & fieri haeredem vitae aeternae. Sed causae certitudinis diversae sunt. Sententiam de numeris mens suo judicio videt. At articuli fidei certi sunt propter revelationem, quae certis & illustribus testimoniis Dei confirmata est, ut resuscitatione mortuorum, & multis aliis miraculis. Sed quia sunt res extra judicium humanae mentis positae, languidior est assensio, quae fit, quia mens movetur illis testimoniis & miraculis, & juvatur a Spiritu sancto ad assentiendum.
